summary:
Across 7 evals (12 iterations), 2 evals ("negative-sagemaker-eval-failed" and "neg-endpoint-autoscaling") were negative-trigger tests that correctly did not fire for either variant, so they were marked skipped for expected-output/assertions/metrics/comparison — this is absent data, not a weakness for either variant.

Of the 5 evals with substantive data, the trigger fired in 100% of cases for both variants in every eval where it was measured.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in all 5 scored evals (mostly high confidence). without_skill matched expected output in 3 of 5 evals ("training-job-failed-internal-error", "tr-execution-role-s3" — at medium confidence, and "reg-approval-gate-missing"), but did not match in 2 evals ("tr-checkpoint-not-resuming" and "reg-auto-registration-off"). In those two evals, without_skill's assertion and comparison data came back null/inconclusive (not scorable), so no assertion-level or quality comparison could be made for without_skill there — this is a case of missing data rather than a confirmed failure on every individual assertion.

Assertion-level results, where both variants had data (3 of the 5 scored evals): many individual assertions passed for both variants (e.g., reading FailureReason, checking CloudWatch logs, not over-attributing failure cause, considering KMS/bucket policy, naming the gating mechanism) — these assertions aren't differentiating the variants. In each of these three evals, with_skill passed all assertions (6/6, 6/6, 7/7) while without_skill passed a subset (4/6, 5/6, 5/7). The assertions where without_skill fell short and with_skill passed included: reporting billed GPU time for a failed job, not exposing a raw account ID (one instance), naming a specific check ID (LLM-SM-TRAIN-005 and LLM-SM-REG-002), and correctly scoping an approval gate to the deployed model version rather than any approved version in the group. No assertion was observed where without_skill passed and with_skill failed.

Quality comparison (LLM-judged, pairwise): in all 3 evals where pairs could be compared, judges favored with_skill over without_skill on accuracy and completeness (without_skill was never favored), with actionability rated comparable in one eval. Confidence on these quality judgments was high in two evals and medium in one. Two evals had quality comparison skipped (1 pair skipped each) due to without_skill's missing/null data.

Runtime and cost: with_skill consistently took longer and cost more (e.g., 37s/$0.31 vs 23s/$0.20; 13s/$0.11 vs 0s/$0.00; 21s/$0.18 vs 0s/$0.00; 22s/$0.19 vs 0s/$0.00; 14s/$0.12 vs 9s/$0.08). Several of without_skill's runtime/cost figures were recorded as 0s/$0.00, which aligns with the evals where without_skill's deeper outputs were not captured/scorable — suggesting measurement gaps for without_skill in those cases rather than necessarily an instant, free response. No runtime threshold overages were recorded for either variant in the evals where thresholds applied.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was not computed for either variant in any eval (all null), so no statement can be made about consistency across repeated runs.

Overall, in the evals with complete paired data, with_skill showed higher expected-output match, higher assertion pass rates, and quality judgments favoring it on accuracy/completeness, at a cost of longer runtime and higher dollar cost. In two evals, without_skill's data was missing/null, which limits confidence in directly comparing those cases and should be treated as a gap in measurement rather than a demonstrated weakness on every criterion. Two further evals were not applicable (correctly non-triggering) for both variants.

training-job-failed-internal-error.summary:
This evaluation is based on a single task instance (one trigger/expected-output pair, one quality comparison pair), so all findings should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected (1/1), and both without_skill and with_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, 100%, with zero low-confidence judgments on either side) — this dimension does not differentiate them.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 6/6 assertions, while without_skill passed 4/6 (67%). Breaking this down:
- Four assertions passed for both variants with high confidence (reading FailureReason, checking CloudWatch logs before concluding, not attributing failure to unsupported causes, and recommending rather than performing a resubmission/support case). These are not differentiating — both variants handled them well.
- Two assertions diverged, both failing for without_skill and passing for with_skill: (1) reporting the billed GPU time (BillableTimeInSeconds) for the failed run, an LLM-judged assertion with high confidence, and (2) not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID, a regex-based (objective) check. The account-ID exposure in particular is a concrete, deterministic finding — without_skill's output in this run included a raw account ID where with_skill's did not.

Quality comparison: Across the one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three judged criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with high average confidence, and without_skill was not favored on any. No criteria were rated comparable. This aligns directionally with the assertion gaps above (missing billing detail, account ID exposure).

Cost and runtime: without_skill was faster (~23s vs ~37s, about 14s less) and cheaper (~$0.20 vs ~$0.31). Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold tracked in the comparison metadata (that threshold metric only flagged 0 of 1 pairs regardless). Context window utilization was low for both (without_skill 4.9%, with_skill 7.3%), with no compaction events for either.

Consistency: Output consistency data is null/absent for both variants, so no conclusion can be drawn about run-to-run stability for either.

Overall shape of the evidence: this is a single-task comparison where without_skill was notably faster and cheaper, but in this instance it missed two specific checks (a billing-detail assertion and a data-exposure/PII-style regex check) that with_skill satisfied, and independent quality judgments favored with_skill on accuracy, actionability, and completeness for this one pair. Given the very small sample (n=1 task), this should be treated as a suggestive but limited finding rather than a definitive characterization of either variant.

tr-execution-role-s3.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (one trigger that fired successfully) comparing with_skill and without_skill on diagnosing an S3/KMS permission issue tied to the LLM-SM-TRAIN-005 check.

Expected output: Both variants met the expected output (1/1), though with_skill's match was rated with high confidence and without_skill's with medium confidence, meaning the measurement behind without_skill's "pass" is somewhat less certain.

Assertions (6 total): Variant_a passed all 6/6 (100%). Variant_b passed 5/6 (83%). Four of the six assertions passed for both variants identically (covering KMS/bucket policy considerations, naming the specific permission to change, avoiding a blanket S3 grant recommendation, and not exposing a raw account ID) — these do not differentiate the variants. One assertion (the KMS key policy must allow the training execution role) also passed for both. The one assertion that differentiated them was a regex check for whether the response explicitly names the "LLM-SM-TRAIN-005" check: with_skill passed this, without_skill did not. This is a single, concrete, low-ambiguity (regex-based) point of difference rather than a broad quality gap.

Quality comparison: Based on one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored across all three judged criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with no criterion favoring without_skill and none rated comparable. This judgment carries only medium average confidence and is based on just one pair, so it should be treated as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a robust pattern.

Metrics: Variant_a took ~13s and cost ~$0.11 per run with 6.6% context utilization; without_skill was recorded at ~0s runtime and ~$0.00 cost with 4.4% context utilization. No runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold for the one pair evaluated. The large runtime/cost gap is notable, but with only one pair evaluated it's unclear how representative this is, and it should be weighed alongside with_skill's advantages on the quality and naming-specificity front rather than viewed in isolation.

Output consistency: No consistency data was available for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability.

Overall, this is a single-task, low-sample-size comparison. On the handful of signals available, with_skill showed an edge (full assertion pass rate, an explicit named-check match, and favored quality judgments), while without_skill was faster and cheaper per the recorded metrics. Given only one pair evaluated and medium/low-ish confidence on several of the differentiating judgments, these results should be read as a limited snapshot rather than a strong, generalizable conclusion.

reg-approval-gate-missing.summary:
This evaluation is based on a single chat task, so all findings rest on a very small sample (one pair evaluated) and should be read as indicative rather than conclusive.

Trigger and expected output: The triggering behavior fired successfully, and both without_skill and with_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, high confidence for both), so this dimension shows no difference between them.

Assertions: This is where the two variants diverge. Both passed 5 of the same 7 assertions identically (naming the approval-status gating mechanism, being explicit that the registry records but doesn't enforce approval, giving concrete wiring to block unapproved deployment, naming the specific ModelApprovalStatus values and gating logic, and not exposing a raw account ID) — these assertions pass for both and so don't differentiate them. However, without_skill failed two assertions that with_skill passed: (1) explicitly naming the "LLM-SM-REG-002" check (a regex-based check), and (2) stating that approval must be checked against the specific deployed model package version rather than any Approved version in the group (an LLM-judged check, scored with high confidence). This gave with_skill a 7/7 (100%) assertion pass rate versus without_skill's 5/7 (71%).

Quality comparison: Across the one pair evaluated, with_skill was favored on two of three criteria (accuracy and completeness) and the two were comparable on the third (actionability). No criterion favored without_skill. This aligns directionally with the assertion gap (missing a named check and a version-specificity nuance would plausibly affect accuracy/completeness). The confidence on this quality judgment is medium, so it's a real but not highly certain signal.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was faster (9s vs 14s) and cheaper ($0.08 vs $0.12), with lower context-window utilization (4.6% vs 6.8%); neither showed any compaction events or exceeded the runtime threshold. This represents a real efficiency advantage for without_skill, to be weighed against the completeness/accuracy gaps noted above rather than treated as decisive on its own.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall, this single-task evaluation shows a tradeoff: without_skill was quicker and cheaper but missed two specific assertions (a named check and a version-specificity detail) and was rated lower on accuracy/completeness in the one quality comparison; with_skill was slower and more costly but more complete/accurate in this instance. Given the sample size of one task, these differences are suggestive rather than statistically robust.
